description: Hedefimiz, Nasa Space Apps'te ilerleyip neler yapabileceğimizi görmek.
summary:
AstroVitals is a health dashboard for the people on the ground who look after astronauts, not for the astronauts themselves. Everything on it comes from sensors the crew already wears or that are built into the cabin: heart rate and ECG, breathing, blood oxygen, blood pressure, temperature and glucose, plus cabin CO₂, oxygen pressure, cabin pressure and radiation. Nobody has to type anything in.

Most monitoring tools quietly assume the data is live. On Mars it isn’t. A reading can be up to 24 minutes old, and for about two weeks during solar conjunction nothing gets through at all. So we built around that. The dashboard estimates what is probably happening right now, tells you whether a problem looks like the person or the habitat, and gives a short catch-up summary when the link comes back. It can also turn an astronaut’s vitals into sound, so a busy controller hears trouble before they see it. Every alert color is tied to a published threshold (NEWS2, ACC/AHA, ADA, NASA-STD-3001), because on a long mission the ground team has to be able to trust what the screen tells them.
details:
What it does

AstroVitals is a monitoring screen for flight surgeons and mission controllers. You pick an astronaut from the top bar and see their state at a glance:

  • a banner that sums up how serious things are, with suggested next steps;
  • a consciousness strip;
  • eight live vital-sign tiles: heart rate, ECG rhythm, breathing, blood oxygen, blood pressure, temperature, glucose and radiation dose;
  • four habitat tiles: cabin CO₂, inspired oxygen, cabin pressure and dose rate.

Double-clicking any tile opens its history, normal range and the source of its threshold. The early-warning banner uses NEWS2, the score UK hospitals use to catch a patient who is getting worse. Blood pressure, glucose, atmosphere and radiation follow ACC/AHA, ADA and NASA-STD-3001. Where we had to set a level ourselves, the app says so. The astronaut never types anything: every value comes from wearable or cabin sensors that have flown or been tested on the ISS, such as the Astroskin bio-monitor shirt, a continuous glucose monitor, a forehead core-temperature sensor and a dry-EEG headband.

What makes it different

We started from one fact: on Mars, the ground is always looking at the past. A signal takes 4 to 24 minutes each way, and during solar conjunction the link is gone for about two weeks. So we added four things a normal dashboard doesn’t have:

  1. Probable value now. One click switches every tile from the last value received to an estimate of what is happening right now. The estimate uses the short-term trend and an uncertainty band that widens with the delay. In our cabin-leak demo, oxygen pressure still reads normal, but the estimate is already in caution, 12 minutes before that data would arrive.
  2. Person or habitat? The app compares everyone in the same cabin against their own baseline and against the cabin sensors. A fever in one astronaut is personal. Two astronauts losing oxygen at the same time as cabin pressure falls points to the ship.
  3. Blackout mode. When conjunction starts, the screen goes cold and says contact is lost. When the link returns, a 14-day summary shows only what changed, like a CO₂ spike, a solar particle event, short nights or rising blood pressure, and passes over everything that stayed stable in one line.
  4. Audio monitoring. Each astronaut gets their own chord. Every heartbeat plays the next note, the chord swells with each breath, and it drifts out of tune as values leave normal. Hospitals are studying this kind of sound to fight alarm fatigue. We think it fits a control room where nobody can stare at one screen all day.

Why it matters

On deep-space missions, crews will have to handle many emergencies on their own. The ground team’s job shifts from reacting in real time to understanding fast and helping where it still can. AstroVitals is built for that job. It shows what is probably happening now, separates medical problems from life-support problems, and gets a team back up to speed after days of silence.

How we built it

The prototype is a single web page written in HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks. Sound comes from the browser’s Web Audio API. Sensor streams are simulated from published baselines, so no real crew data is used. A test panel can trigger scenarios such as fainting, atrial fibrillation, fever, hypoxia, a cabin leak, a CO₂ rise, a solar storm and solar conjunction. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write code and polish text, with the organizers’ approval.

What we paid attention to

  • Red means warning and amber means caution, following the aviation rule (14 CFR 25.1322).
  • Every status also has a shape and a word, so color-blind users can read it.
  • Text contrast is at least 5:1.
  • The app works in light and dark themes, in English and Turkish, and respects the system’s reduced-motion setting.
  • We were honest about limits. NEWS2 has not been validated in astronauts, resting body temperature runs about 1 °C higher in space, and the prototype runs on simulated data. Next, we want flight surgeons to review the thresholds and we want to connect real telemetry.
